Introduction

If you have read my recent rant about programming languages, you'll know I've been quite interested in Gleam. Gleam is a functional language that targets BEAM, the Erlang VM,1 with a simple syntax and interoperability with the wider BEAM ecosystem (Erlang and Elixir). Interestingly, Gleam can also target JavaScript i.e., Gleam can be compiled into JavaScript and run through Node.js.

I've been mostly using Rust for hobby projects, which at the moment is the only language that really makes coding enjoyable for me, and Gleam has managed to scratch that itch too. If you're a Rust connaisseur, then Gleam will feel familiar to you, bar a few key differences. I feel like 80% of the code I write could be copy pasted to Rust (with a tinge of search-and-replace for syntax) and it'd compile.

This post won't give an exhaustive overview of the language, if you want to learn more, I recommend the excellent interactive tour. You'll get a good feel for Gleam in under half an hour.

Gleam: the good

On its homepage, Gleam is described as "a friendly language for building type-safe systems that scale!" (emphasis theirs) which does a good job of conveying what Gleam is all about.

Gleam is friendly

The syntax is extremely simple, most of the complex stuff is hidden by the Erlang runtime which you don't really have to interact with unless you want to! Of course, Gleam is a functional language, so if you have lived in a C-shaped imperative world your whole life, it might be a bit daunting at first. But if you compare it to other functional languages (OCaml, Haskell, Erlang), you'll quickly notice Gleam is much simpler. After using it a bit, it feels like all the functional parts of Rust, with a few missing ones, and none of the imperative parts.

Let's start from an example piece of code:

Dissecting this a bit, you can see a few specificities of Gleam:

  • variables in Gleam are immutable (so no mut keyword or anything like that), chained functions here all return a new element.2 You can still shadow a binding with a new let, which is how you "update" a value.
  • |> (typed |>) is the pipe operator used to chain functions on data. The main constraint is that the piped variable should be the first argument of the function in the pipe.
  • just like Rust, errors in Gleam are just values as part of the Result monad.3

Comparing with the Rust code snippet, you can see that, up to a few naming choices, they look pretty similar. The main difference in this example is really the piping vs. chaining syntax. Gleam types have no methods so piping is used instead.

The piping operator |> is the first of the three mascot features of Gleam you will meet in this post, the other two being the use pattern and tail-call optimization.

The use pattern

If you've written a lot of JavaScript, you might be used to the indentation creep that arises when nesting many callbacks into one another

someFunc(arg, function(param) {
  someOtherFunc(param, function(otherParam) {
    // ...
  })
})

In Gleam, many functions expect a callback, for example because as a way to control access to a resource and clean up when the process is done (closing a database connection, releasing a file handle, etc.). To avoid this kind of tower of callbacks, Gleam provides some syntactic sugar: use param <- some_func(arg) is equivalent to some_func(arg, fn(param) { ... }). The callback must always be the last argument of the function. That is the opposite of |>, which fills the first one.

Tail-call optimization

This one might genuinely trip you up if you're not familiar with it. The first thing you need to know is there are no loops in Gleam! Again, if you've written OCaml or Haskell before, you won't be surprised by this. In 98% of cases,4 loops are simple operations over bounded iterations. Think for loops on a list or a set. Exactly the kind of thing which in Rust you always have two ways of doing: one imperative with the exact for loop, one more functional with a combination of operations on iterators. Well, if you look at the code example in the previous section, you'll see Gleam uses the second kind and has a plethora of functions to iterate over lists, sets, tuples, strings, anything.

But what if you need something more complicated? What about the 2%? This is where you would instead use recursion! A simple algorithm which illustrates this is Euclid's algorithm to compute the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD). Below you can find a Rust iterative example, and a Gleam recursive example.

Of course, you can also write the recursive version in Rust, but this usually isn't such a great idea. Recursion in imperative languages can quickly get out of hand: every call adds a new stack frame, and a deeply recursive function can blow the stack (the infamous stack overflow).

On the BEAM there is no fixed-size stack, so runaway recursion eats heap memory until the process is killed instead, but the point remains: deep recursions equals trouble. To avoid that problem, compilers for functional languages implement a technique called Tail Call Optimization (TCO), which applies when the recursive call is the last thing the function does. The existing stack frame is then reused instead of stacking a new one, giving performance close to an imperative while loop.5

Gleam is type-safe

This piece of the slogan is mostly there to answer the obvious question "why Gleam and not Elixir?" (another Erlang-based language). While Elixir is a dynamically-typed language (with gradual typing now!), Gleam was built as a statically-typed language with a strong type system: strong types are its raison d'être.

A type in Gleam encompasses both the enum and the struct concepts in Rust:

Because Gleam types are algebraic data types, they are very useful to ensure undesired states are impossible. A great aspect of Gleam, which will be relevant a little bit later, is that it compiles to both the BEAM virtual machine and to JavaScript. So you can share these strong type definitions across different applications in both targets. This is particularly handy if you need a web application to communicate with a BEAM app.

Gleam is made for systems that scale

That, of course, refers to BEAM, the Erlang VM. Unlike languages which target the native system (Rust, Go, C++), a VM provides an extra abstraction layer between the system and the program. In the case of BEAM, that layer is exceptionally good at handling concurrent processes and failures while remaining fast.

Gleam makes good use of that, and this is what a concurrent program would look like:

// Omitted imports
pub fn main() {
  let order_number_and_amounts = [
    #(101, 100),
    #(102, 200),
    #(103, 300)
  ]
  
  order_number_and_amounts
  |> list.each(fn(x) {
    let #(order_no, amount) = x
    let order_description = "Order #" <> int.to_string(order_no)

    // Spawn unlinked: a crashing worker must not take the parent down.
    process.spawn_unlinked(fn() {
      // 101 and 103 will succeed, 102 will crash
      process_order(order_description, amount)
    })
  })

  io.println("All orders dispatched!")

  // Keep the parent alive until the children have had time to run.
  process.sleep(10)
}

fn process_order(order: String, amount: Int) {
  process.sleep(1)
  case amount {
    200 -> panic as "Payment failed!"
    _ -> io.println(order <> " processed successfully")
  }
}

// Stdout
// ----
// All orders dispatched!
// Order #101 processed successfully
// Order #103 processed successfully

What you should take away from this code is that it's the BEAM that handles processes.

The call to process.spawn_unlinked triggers a new process with no link to its creator, so when order 102 crashes, neither the parent nor siblings are affected. With a plain process.spawn the child would be linked to the caller, and that panic would have taken the whole program down. If you look closely, I also added process.sleep(10) so the parent wouldn't close before the children could finish: this is a hack, since the delay is only a guess and a slower child would still be cut off.

Thankfully, a great advantage of the BEAM is how easy inter-process communication is, which the following code piece illustrates well:

// Omitted imports
pub type PaymentError {
  PaymentFailed
}

pub fn main() {
  let parent = process.new_subject()
  let orders = [
    #(101, False),
    #(102, True),
    #(103, False)
  ]

  orders
  |> list.each(fn(x) {
    let #(order_no, should_fail) = x

    process.spawn(fn() {
      // Simulate processing time
      process.sleep(1000)

      // 101 and 103 succeed, 102 fails
      let res = case should_fail {
        True -> Error(PaymentFailed)
        False -> Ok(Nil)
      }

      process.send(parent, #(order_no, res))
    })
  })

  io.println("All orders dispatched!")

  receive_results(list.length(orders), parent)
}

fn receive_results(
  remaining: Int,
  parent: process.Subject(#(Int, Result(Nil, PaymentError))),
) -> Nil {
  case remaining {
    0 -> Nil

    _ -> {
      let #(order_no, res) = process.receive_forever(parent)

      let status = case res {
        Ok(_) -> "successful"
        Error(_) -> "failed"
      }

      io.println(
        "Processing of order #" <> int.to_string(order_no) <> " " <> status <> "!",
      )

      receive_results(remaining - 1, parent)
    }
  }
}

// Stdout
// ----
// All orders dispatched!
// Processing of order #103 successful!
// Processing of order #102 failed!
// Processing of order #101 successful!
//
// The order of the last three lines depends on scheduling.

OTP: the gift that keeps on giving

In the paragraph above, I briefly showed how the BEAM virtual machine is great for concurrent programs communicating by message passing. If you're familiar with Go, this is similar to how it handles the same problem with goroutines. But the OTP (Open Telecom Platform), the set of libraries that ships with Erlang, is more powerful than that. It provides you with a built-in supervisor-actor paradigm which enables you to create scalable, concurrent services which can crash without taking down the whole application.

In a nutshell, the OTP exposes actors: lightweight processes that hold state and communicate with each other via messages (like in the example above). When paired with a supervisor, the whole application becomes more resilient to any individual actor crashing: the supervisor will monitor processes and restart them as needed. It can also help start/stop groups of actors dynamically.

If you're reading this and thinking "uh that sounds a lot like how I used Kubernetes", you're not alone. The OTP model is extremely similar to the controller-pod architecture of Kubernetes and solves a lot of the same problems.6 However, in my experience, a lot of workflows using Kubernetes don't really need a cluster but still use one (and that's expensive!) because of the added bonus of the distributive experience. For those cases, the OTP provides a really interesting alternative.

Let me give you a concrete example. Without going in too much detail, we have a common setup in my team which involves a handwritten Go job scheduler handling some other processes.

The scheduler, each worker, and the user interface are all pods inside the cluster, managed by Kubernetes. To be honest, this works well, but it does introduce a lot of complexity. First of all, most of these services do not need to be so isolated from each other. The consequence here is that we need duplicate REST APIs in various places to enable communication between different services.

What if we wanted to reorganize this within a Gleam application? There are two parts where Gleam would shine here:

  1. the OTP would essentially unify all scheduling services as actors within a single application,
  2. the user interface (currently a Node.js app) can be written in Gleam and compiled to JavaScript.

Here is the revised architecture:

Within the BEAM application, all actors would communicate via messages:

  • the HTTP server receives requests and saves them to the DB,
  • the workers would pick up jobs and write the status back to the DB.

So instead of handling the deployment of multiple applications in separate pods, you can just let the OTP handle all process management within one VM (for the scheduling part).

What does it mean to reuse code between the frontend and the backend?

As mentioned before, one of the big advantages of Gleam is that it compiles to JavaScript. So you can bundle shared type definitions between the user interface and the job scheduler instead of keeping duplicate APIs in sync.

Gleam: the bad

Every language has its flaws, and it's time for some honest feedback on Gleam. I don't pretend I have much experience with the language yet, so if any of these complaints feel unfair to you, feel free to correct me. So far, these are the things I noticed:

  • the ecosystem is small. This is not Gleam's fault per se, just a consequence of being a young language,7 and there are mitigating factors such as the possibility to use external functions quite easily (Erlang, Elixir on BEAM, JavaScript on its own runtime) directly from Gleam. Yet, the community itself favours Gleam-first packages and as of today, there are some gaps in package variety.
  • The language is too simple. Well, to be honest I don't agree per se with this, I like it like this. But I totally understand that the lack of macros or other complex features can put a few people off (for example, I read that currying is dearly missed).
  • The BEAM virtual machine is an excellent target, but it's also a peculiarity. I couldn't really name any big company/system using it. Yet, a quick search shows that WhatsApp, Discord and Pinterest, as well as Cisco, Nintendo, and even the NHS rely on it. Erlang and BEAM are quietly powering huge platforms due to their reliability, but it's not as flashy as "Made in Rust" marketing. Where Rust had Mozilla, Go had Google and Java had Oracle, there isn't a big tech player pushing for Gleam/Erlang right now.

Of course this is a very biased account. I think I'm missing a lot of flaws in the language itself, flaws that will show themselves once the honeymoon period is over. But for now, I'm having a blast with Gleam, and I can only encourage you to give it a try too! I'm sure just like me, you'll have a lot of fun!

item.title: What is malloc doing, anyway? (187 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://benmandrew.com/articles/what-is-malloc-doing-anyway, See on Hacker News

malloc has a very nice and simple interface: you ask for a certain amount of memory, and you’re given a void pointer to your block of contiguous bytes that’s been magicked into existence. Once you’re done with it, you call free with the same pointer and the memory disappears into the ether.

But what’s actually happening here? Obviously, as we’re running as a userspace program, malloc must be asking the kernel for the memory through syscalls. However, we may be allocating many small blocks, and syscalls are expensive (575 ns for an empty one, as measured below), so some bookkeeping is done in the background. We’ll demonstrate this on GNU libc (glibc) with the program snippet below, which calls malloc(16) a thousand times.

static void *ptrs[1000];

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
        ptrs[i] = malloc(16);
}

Using strace, we can see that the whole loop makes only two brk syscalls: the first asks where the program break is (the address where the process’s heap ends), and the second grows the heap by 132 KiB. These are both done in the first malloc call — the other 999 just take from that already allocated memory.

$ strace -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap,write \
    ./malloc1000 > /dev/null
...
brk(NULL)              = 0x59faca231000
brk(0x59faca252000)    = 0x59faca252000
+++ exited with 0 +++

You may see both brk and sbrk mentioned in discussions. brk is a syscall that sets the program break to the address it is provided, and sbrk is a libc convenience wrapper that takes a delta, increasing the program break by that amount.

The Address Space

A running process gets its own address space, split into a number of regions. These include text for executable code, data for initialised global variables, and bss for uninitialised global variables, among others. The following program prints one address from each region of the process.

#define SHOW(label, p) \
    printf("%-22s %p\n", label, (void *)(p))

SHOW("main (text)", main);
SHOW("initialised (data)", &initialised);
SHOW("uninitialised (bss)", &uninitialised);
SHOW("malloc(16) (heap)", malloc(16));
SHOW("program break", sbrk(0));
SHOW("printf (libc)", printf);
SHOW("local (stack)", &local);

The addresses rise from the binary’s code up to its stack.

$ ./layout
main (text)            0x59c0791d7149
initialised (data)     0x59c0791da020
uninitialised (bss)    0x59c0791da028
malloc(16) (heap)      0x59c0903182b0
program break          0x59c090338000
printf (libc)          0x711dcf7c15b0
local (stack)          0x7ffff86c45ec

Some of these regions can change as the program runs. For example, malloc(16) grows the heap and moves the break up. Note that in this run, the break and printf in libc are 23.4 TiB apart, about 1,530 times the machine’s 15.6 GiB of RAM. Nearly all of that range is unmapped, so it costs no physical memory.

A Toy Allocator with sbrk

Because we can move the program break directly, we can write a little allocator of our own. This is called a bump allocator, because each call simply bumps up the amount of memory that we are allowed to use.

void *my_malloc(size_t size) {
    void *p = sbrk(align_up(size));
    return p == (void *)-1 ? NULL : p;
}

void my_free(void *ptr) {
    (void)ptr;
}

This allocator is not very good! It moves the break on every single request, and each move is a syscall. We can time a syscall against malloc to see why malloc requests large blocks from the kernel and cuts them up itself. Each of the following three functions is timed over a million calls.

static void *volatile sink;

static void call_getppid(void) {
    syscall(SYS_getppid);
}

static void call_sbrk(void) {
    sink = sbrk(16);
}

static void call_malloc(void) {
    sink = malloc(16);
}

sbrk(16) costs only 35 ns more than the empty syscall, whereas malloc(16) runs 22.7 times faster than sbrk(16).

$ ./syscall-cost
syscall(SYS_getppid)      575.2 ns per call
sbrk(16)                  610.1 ns per call
malloc(16)                 26.9 ns per call
sbrk(16) / malloc(16)      22.7x

The bump allocator also has no way to reuse freed memory. Each request lands straight after the one before, so in the following example, d goes after c even though b has been freed.

$ ./my-bump-1
a = my_malloc(16)   start+0
b = my_malloc(1)    start+16
c = my_malloc(100)  start+32
my_free(b)
d = my_malloc(1)    start+144
break               start+160

The rest of the post improves the allocator one stage at a time.

Chunks and Headers

malloc actually allocates more memory than you request. This is because each allocation, or chunk, has a size header just before the returned pointer; this is how free works without passing an explicit size. Chunk sizes are always multiples of 16, so the low bits of the size are always zero, and glibc keeps three flags in them.

size_t requests[] = {1, 24, 25, 1000};

size_t count = sizeof requests / sizeof requests[0];
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    char *p = malloc(requests[i]);
    size_t chunk = ((size_t *)p)[-1] & ~(size_t)7;
    printf("%8zu %8zu\n", requests[i], chunk);
}

Each chunk is the request plus 8 bytes for the header, rounded up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum of 32. The rounding keeps every pointer that malloc returns 16-byte aligned, which is the alignment x86-64 gives max_align_t, so the memory suits any C type. The 32-byte minimum leaves room for the list pointers that a chunk stores once it is freed.

$ ./chunk-header
 request    chunk
       1       32
      24       32
      25       48
    1000     1008

When we free a chunk, it is put into what’s called a free list to allow reuse. When more data is requested, malloc looks through this free list and splits large chunks to fit small requests, and free merges free neighbours back together. Each chunk in the free list needs two pieces of information: its size (which we already have), and a pointer to the next chunk in the free list. glibc stores the pointer after the size, reusing the memory that the user stored their data in before it was freed!

The toy allocator stores the same two fields in each chunk.

typedef struct chunk {
    size_t size;
    struct chunk *next;
} chunk_t;

Splitting and Coalescing

We can improve our my_malloc by rounding the request plus its header up to a multiple of 16 bytes, and taking the first chunk in the free list that is big enough. To keep things simple, the toy’s header is the whole chunk_t, so a chunk keeps room for next even while it is in use. That makes the header 16 bytes where glibc’s is 8, and my_malloc(100) takes a 128-byte chunk where malloc(100) takes 112.

void *my_malloc(size_t size) {
    size_t need = align_up(size + HEADER_SIZE, ALIGN);
    for (chunk_t **link = &free_list; *link != NULL;
         link = &(*link)->next)
        if ((*link)->size >= need)
            return take(link, need);
    if (grow_heap(need) != 0)
        return NULL;
    return my_malloc(size);
}

We define take to split that chunk, leaving whatever the request does not need in the free list.

static void *take(chunk_t **link, size_t need) {
    chunk_t *c = *link;
    if (c->size > need) {
        chunk_t *rest = (chunk_t *)((char *)c + need);
        rest->size = c->size - need;
        rest->next = c->next;
        c->size = need;
        *link = rest;
    } else {
        *link = c->next;
    }
    return (char *)c + HEADER_SIZE;
}

When no free chunk fits, grow_heap moves the program break up in 64 KiB steps using sbrk and puts the new space on the free list as one chunk.

With headers, we can now actually implement a proper my_free function! It steps back from the pointer to the header and hands the chunk c to insert_free. That function walks the list to find the free chunks either side of c by address, prev and next, and links c in between them. Then, if c ends where next starts, or starts where prev ends, the two become one chunk.

if (next != NULL && (char *)c + c->size == (char *)next) {
    c->size += next->size;
    c->next = next->next;
}
if (prev != NULL && (char *)prev + prev->size == (char *)c) {
    prev->size += c->size;
    prev->next = c->next;
}

A test program allocates a, b and c, frees a and b, allocates d, then frees the rest.

Each line shows the chunk that the call allocated, if any, and then the free list. Every chunk is an [offset, size] pair counted from the start of the heap, and the offset is where its header starts, 16 bytes before the pointer that my_malloc returns.

$ ./my-freelist-2
a = my_malloc(100)   [0, 128]     free: [128, 65408]
b = my_malloc(200)   [128, 224]   free: [352, 65184]
c = my_malloc(100)   [352, 128]   free: [480, 65056]
my_free(a)                        free: [0, 128] [480, 65056]
my_free(b)                        free: [0, 352] [480, 65056]
d = my_malloc(50)    [0, 80]      free: [80, 272] [480, 65056]
my_free(c)                        free: [80, 65456]
my_free(d)                        free: [0, 65536]

d gets the chunk at offset 0, split from the 352-byte chunk that a and b merged into. The bump allocator put its fourth request after everything else. Freeing c merges three chunks into one, and freeing d leaves the single 64 KiB chunk that grow_heap added.

Demand Paging

my_free reuses memory, but it never returns any to the kernel. Whether a free chunk still costs RAM depends on when the kernel puts physical memory behind an address. Each process sees virtual memory, which the kernel maps onto physical RAM in 4 KiB pages. That separation allows the kernel to hand out address ranges with no physical RAM behind them — a virtual page only needs to be backed by physical memory on its first write.

The following program moves the break up by 1 GiB, then writes one byte to every page and prints a row after each 256 MiB.

char *p = sbrk(SIZE);
print_row(0);
for (size_t offset = 0; offset < SIZE; offset += PAGE_SIZE) {
    p[offset] = 1;
    if ((offset + PAGE_SIZE) % (SIZE / 4) == 0)
        print_row((long)((offset + PAGE_SIZE) >> 20));
}

Virtual size counts the addresses the process has mapped, and resident set size (RSS) counts the pages that are in RAM. Straight after sbrk, virtual size is already just over 1 GiB, while RSS is 1308 KiB. Each 256 MiB written then costs 65,536 page faults, one per 4 KiB page, increasing the RSS.

$ ./demand-paging
   written     faults        virtual       resident
     0 MiB          3    1050916 KiB       1308 KiB
   256 MiB      65539    1050916 KiB     263536 KiB
   512 MiB     131075    1050916 KiB     525680 KiB
   768 MiB     196611    1050916 KiB     787824 KiB
  1024 MiB     262147    1050916 KiB    1049968 KiB

Once a chunk’s pages have been written, they stay resident after my_free, until the allocator gives them back to the kernel.

Giving Memory Back

We give memory back to the kernel by lowering the break. We introduce a new function, trim, that lowers the break once the free chunk at the top of the heap reaches 128 KiB, keeping 64 KiB so that the next few requests don’t move the break straight back up.

static void trim(void) {
    chunk_t *top = free_list;
    if (top == NULL)
        return;
    while (top->next != NULL)
        top = top->next;
    char *end = (char *)top + top->size;
    if (end != (char *)sbrk(0) || top->size < TRIM_THRESHOLD)
        return;
    size_t release =
        (top->size - TOP_PAD) / PAGE_SIZE * PAGE_SIZE;
    top->size -= release;
    sbrk(-(intptr_t)release);
}

A test program allocates 1 MiB and then a 16-byte chunk above it, then writes to every page of the 1 MiB block. (Anonymous RSS counts resident memory with no backing file, which keeps libc’s code out of the numbers.)

$ ./my-trim-3
                                 break         anonymous RSS
my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16)  start+1088 KiB     1124 KiB
my_free(1 MiB)                   start+1088 KiB     1124 KiB
my_free(16)                      start+64 KiB        160 KiB

Freeing the 1 MiB block leaves the break at 1088 KiB and anonymous RSS at 1124 KiB, because the 16-byte chunk above it is still live. Once that chunk goes too, trim lowers the break to 64 KiB, dropping the anonymous RSS to 160 KiB.

Only the top of the heap can be given back. A live chunk holds the break above it, so every free chunk below it stays resident, as the 1 MiB block did here. Over a long run, many allocations and deallocations leave free gaps between live chunks that later requests rarely fill, which is called fragmentation. These gaps stay resident, so in a long-running program, fragmentation can grow RSS until a memory limit kills the process.

Large Blocks with mmap

The mmap syscall usually maps a file into the address space. With the MAP_ANONYMOUS flag there is no backing file, and the kernel creates a zero-filled, page-aligned mapping anywhere in the address space. Like the heap, its resident pages count towards the anonymous RSS. The munmap syscall returns a block with its own mapping to the kernel as soon as it is freed, whatever lies next to it.

To integrate this into our own allocator, my_malloc chooses between sbrk and mmap by the size of the request. Any request of 128 KiB or more, header included, gets a mapping of its own from map_chunk, rounded up to whole pages; smaller requests take the existing sbrk free list path.

static void *map_chunk(size_t need) {
    size_t len = align_up(need, PAGE_SIZE);
    chunk_t *c = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
                      MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
    if (c == MAP_FAILED)
        return NULL;
    c->size = len | MMAPPED; // chunk is mapped
    return (char *)c + HEADER_SIZE;
}

For mmapped chunks, we use one of the three flags in the size header (M) to record that this chunk has its own mapping. my_free checks this bit to know how to free it. It unmaps a mapped chunk with munmap, and puts any other chunk back on the free list, where trim can release it.

void my_free(void *ptr) {
    if (ptr == NULL)
        return;
    chunk_t *c = (chunk_t *)((char *)ptr - HEADER_SIZE);
    if (c->size & MMAPPED) {
        munmap(c, c->size & ~(size_t)MMAPPED);
        return;
    }
    insert_free(c);
    trim();
}

Running the previous demo again, we see that freeing the 1 MiB block drops the anonymous RSS while the 16-byte chunk is still live.

$ ./my-mmap-4
                                 break         anonymous RSS
my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16)  start+64 KiB       1128 KiB
my_free(1 MiB)                   start+64 KiB        100 KiB
my_free(16)                      start+64 KiB        100 KiB

The following diagram shows how this might look in the address space.

Why not mmap everything? Some allocators do! Even glibc creates extra heaps, called arenas, with mmap, and spreads threads across them so that they don’t all contend for the lock on the main heap. However, separate mappings have separate regions with no guarantee of contiguity, and chunks can’t be coalesced across these gaps. On the other hand, allocating with sbrk just bumps up the one contiguous region that you already have. A freed chunk that stays on the heap keeps its pages resident, so reusing it causes no page faults. Each new mapping starts with no physical memory behind it, and faults on every page it writes.

Comparing Performance

We compare the performance of our allocators against glibc’s malloc with a workload that repeatedly allocates and deallocates blocks of varying sizes1. To measure the speed, we find the average time of a step: free a random live block, allocate a replacement of random size, and write to each of its pages. At the end of the run, the live blocks hold 10.3 MiB. The last two columns give the anonymous RSS at that point, and again after every block is freed, which is the memory the allocator keeps.

my-bump-1 never frees or reuses memory, so its RSS is the 1425 MiB that the run allocates in total. Its 1.72 µs per step comes from an sbrk call for every request and page faults on new pages. my-freelist-2 reuses memory, so its RSS of 17.8 MiB is much closer to the 10.3 MiB of live data. However, each step walks the list twice: my_malloc walks it to find a fit, and insert_free walks it to find the chunk’s neighbours. my-trim-3 adds a third walk, because trim looks for the last free chunk on every my_free. my-freelist-2 and my-trim-3 run 65 and 142 times slower than glibc respectively. In return, my-trim-3 keeps only 0.188 MiB once every block is freed. my-mmap-4 calls mmap for large requests, which raises its time per step to 11.8 µs but gives it the lowest RSS with blocks live, at 11.2 MiB.

Why is glibc so fast? The slowdowns in our allocators are due to having to walk a long free list of chunks multiple times. glibc instead keeps free chunks in bins, separate lists by size, so a request can walk a list of appropriately sized chunks directly. It also keeps up to seven freed chunks of each small size in a thread-local cache (tcache) and hands them straight back to the next request of that size.

The tcache also explains the last column, where glibc keeps 19.0 MiB after every block is freed. The heap counts a cached chunk as in use, so one near the top stops glibc from lowering the break. The GLIBC_TUNABLES environment variable can turn the tcache off with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0, or fix the mmap threshold at 128 KiB with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=131072.

With the tcache off, freeing everything leaves 0.250 MiB, and each step takes 1.5 times as long as before.

glibc makes 51 mmap calls in the whole run, against the 5040 that my-mmap-4 makes. Freeing a mapped chunk raises glibc’s threshold to that chunk’s size, so later large requests come from the heap. With the threshold fixed at 128 KiB, every large request pays for its syscalls and page faults again, and glibc runs 10.7 times slower.

malloc spends memory to stay away from the kernel, parcelling out large blocks in userspace so that most calls never make a syscall.

  • The man pages for brk(2) and sbrk(2) (link), mmap(2) (link), mallopt(3) (link) and malloc_trim(3) (link).

item.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (173 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14162, See on Hacker News

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. Non-English prompts use up to 179 times more energy.

The globalization of AI comes with a massive environmental tax. Building for an international audience just became an infrastructure nightmare.

Researchers at the University of Michigan have uncovered a staggering disparity in AI resource consumption. According to their findings, processing AI prompts in non-English languages consumes up to 179 times more energy than running the exact same prompts in English. Worse, this massive spike in power draw often results in lower accuracy.

This completely shatters the illusion of effortless multilingual AI. If you are building a product intended for a global user base, your compute costs and latency just became wildly unpredictable based entirely on the user's native language. The tokenization systems underlying modern models are heavily optimized for English, punishing everyone else with bloated token counts and agonizingly slow inference.

Agentic AI is a security nightmare waiting to happen, and enterprise defense giants are writing massive checks to plug the holes.

Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in discussions to acquire the cybersecurity startup Clutch for approximately $500 million. The specific goal of this massive proposed buyout is to enhance control over AI agents and strictly manage their access to internal company systems.

We are finally seeing the enterprise reaction to autonomous agents. Everyone wants AI that can take actions on their behalf, but nobody wants a rogue script hallucinating its way into the payroll database. Clutch built the exact guardrails that massive corporations need before they let agentic workflows touch their proprietary data, and Palo Alto is paying a premium to own that chokepoint.

The startups that win will be the ones that can show their AI won't accidentally delete the production database when given a vague prompt.

By productizing exploit generation, OpenAI is acknowledging that the only way to secure the next generation of software is to attack it with the same automated ferocity that malicious actors are already developing.

For working developers, the margin for error just vanished. If a commercially available model can automatically find and exploit vulnerabilities in your codebase, security through obscurity is dead. You now have to assume that every endpoint you expose will be instantly probed by an agent smarter than the engineer who wrote it.

Interrogating your entire workforce about their prompt history is a fast track to losing your best talent.

item.title: A Critique of GPUI (131 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.zortax.de/posts/a-critique-of-gpui, See on Hacker News

Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI.1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on.

To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps.

I want to make two arguments:

  • Every UI architecture ends up needing to know what changed and who depends on it, or performance characteristics will not scale. A framework whose state model cannot say so makes the application say it by hand, at the cost of whatever made that framework’s API semantics attractive in the first place.
  • Once you admit you want that precision, components that run once, with signals and reactive holes, are the simplest API for it.

Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu2, I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui, a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts.

The only question that matters

Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.”3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. So every framework has to answer one question: when one value changes, what runs?

ModelWhat a write runsWho finds the change
Immediate (egui)All UI code, next frameNobody
Elm (Iced)All of view, then a diffThe diff
Views (GPUI)Every view without a cacheYou, with notify
Signals, re-run (Freya, Compose)Components that read itThe framework
Signals, run once (Floem, Solid, zgui)Closures that read itThe framework

I understand why people like the first three. No state to synchronize, one place where state lives, a render function that is plain Rust, no macros or separate compiler. I’m gonna make the argument that these approaches don’t scale, and fixing the underlying problem defeats what makes these models simple and easy to reason about.

GPUI: notify is zone.js

GPUI calls itself “a hybrid immediate and retained mode” framework.4 It retains state in entities. The UI is defined in render functions, changing state must trigger a rerun.

impl Render for Sidebar {
    fn render(
        &mut self,
        _: &mut Window,
        cx: &mut Context<Self>,
    ) -> impl IntoElement {
        let inbox = self.inbox.read(cx);
        div()
            .child(format!("{} unread", inbox.unread()))
            .children(inbox.threads.iter().map(|t| t.title.clone()))
    }
}

It is ordinary Rust. You can use if, for and local variables, and there aren’t any weird wrappers. State changes require an explicit notification:

self.threads[i].unread = false;
cx.notify();

notify carries the entity id.5 Since Rust doesn’t have a write barrier on &mut, GPUI cannot see which field changed (or whether anything changed at all). The Angular team wrote this about zone.js in 2023: it “is only capable of notifying us when something might have happened”, and “This approach has not scaled well.”6 notify is more precise than a zone, since it names an entity, but ultimately it makes the same kind of statement. Below that id, GPUI knows nothing, so it re-renders every view that is not behind a valid .cached() boundary. And in practice, GPUI often rerender every view, because .cached() is rarely used by application authors, and imposes certain restrictions on layout semantics.

GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.

At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).

This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”.7

Making GPUI precise defeats GPUI

The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames.8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:

pub struct UnreadBadge { unread: usize, _watch: Subscription }

impl UnreadBadge {
    pub fn new(inbox: Entity<Inbox>, cx: &mut Context<Self>) -> Self {
        let unread = inbox.read(cx).unread();
        let _watch = cx.observe(&inbox, |this, inbox, cx| {
            let unread = inbox.read(cx).unread();
            if unread != this.unread {
                this.unread = unread;
                cx.notify();
            }
        });
        Self { unread, _watch }
    }
}

impl Render for UnreadBadge {
    fn render(
        &mut self,
        _: &mut Window,
        _: &mut Context<Self>,
    ) -> impl IntoElement {
        format!("{} unread", self.unread)
    }
}

Its owner then has to create it and keep the handle:

let badge = cx.new(|cx| UnreadBadge::new(inbox.clone(), cx));

That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value, a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one count. In a signal framework it is this:

let unread = Memo::new(move |_| {
    threads.with(|ts| ts.iter().filter(|t| t.unread.get()).count())
});
Label::derived(move || format!("{} unread", unread.get()))

The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means managing a keyed map of entities by hand.

And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:

With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”.8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.

The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”.10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”.11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.

This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”.12 Keep the pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a new state model and a new element contract.

Elm: deceptively simple at small scales

At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple UI model: one state value, one update, one view, and every change has a name. While large applications do use it successully,13 14 I do want to make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.

Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:

match message {
    InboxMessage::MarkRead(i) => {
        if self.threads[i].unread {
            self.threads[i].unread = false;
            self.unread -= 1;
        }
    }
    InboxMessage::Delete(i) => {
        if self.threads.remove(i).unread {
            self.unread -= 1;
        }
    }
    InboxMessage::Arrived(thread) => {
        self.unread += thread.unread as usize;
        self.threads.push(thread);
    }
}

The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget it.

The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.”15. Iced recommends returning an Action to the parent.16 Iced’s maintainer says components in this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data model”.17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136 top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that returns commands for the parent to interpret.18 Everything in that is explicit, and none of it is simple.

The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field. Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics.19

This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”.20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”.21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate.22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.”23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style.24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.

Performance follows the same line. Since Iced rebuilds all of view after every batch of messages, one label at 3,000 rows builds 39,023 widgets and takes 7.3 ms. Lazy on every row only gets that to 5.7 ms, because view still has to visit each row to hash its key. The official lazy example keys on a version: u8 that four update arms bump by hand.25 That is a dirty flag with a nicer name. In fairness, cosmic-files and Halloy use no lazy at all, and on a virtualized list Iced is one of the fastest frameworks I measured, at 0.19 ms. A bounded screen rebuilds cheaply. But asymptotic complexity is clear. And similar to GPUI, the API semantics simply can’t express the necessary information.

There is actually precedence for this: Vizia shows what happens when you add precision to this model. It moved from lenses to signals in March 2026 and kept its Model and event dispatch.26 This is its counter, shortened:27

pub enum AppEvent {
    Increment,
}

impl Model for AppData {
    fn event(&mut self, _: &mut EventContext, event: &mut Event) {
        event.map(|app_event, _| match app_event {
            AppEvent::Increment => self.count.update(|count| *count += 1),
        });
    }
}
let count = Signal::new(0);
AppData { count }.build(cx);
Button::new(cx, |cx| Label::new(cx, "Increment"))
    .on_press(|cx| cx.emit(AppEvent::Increment));
Label::new(cx, count).width(Pixels(50.0)).live(Live::Polite);

The label reads the signal directly, and the same closure that builds the button created it. The enum, the dispatch and the handler exist to carry one call to update. Vizia was never strict Elm, since its views are built once, and signals were a sensible move: it got per-field writes. But look at what remains of Elm’s reasons. State is a graph of mutable cells, Model is a bag of handles, and event is a &mut self side effect. You now have two systems for saying that something changed. So my objection to adding signals to the Elm architecture really is the same as with GPUI: they work, and they remove what you came for.

egui’s pitch is the best in the field: “You don’t have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync”.28 For a tool, this is hard to beat:

for row in rows {
    ui.horizontal(|ui| {
        ui.label(&row.name);
        ui.label(row.price.to_string());
        if ui.button("+").clicked() {
            row.price += 1;
        }
    });
}

The price is that a frame costs the size of the UI, independent of what changed. At 3,000 rows every small edit takes about 32 ms, or about 19 ms with accessibility off. egui’s author is candid about the trade: immediate mode is “easier to use, but less powerful”.28

As the application grows, the original attraction goes. The layout paradox is “a fundamental shortcoming”.28 Long lists need show_rows, which takes one fixed row height. Rerun, the largest egui application I know of, clamps queries by “inspecting egui state from the previous frame”.29 Anything expensive goes behind a cache keyed on your data. A cache that has to agree with your data is the synchronization problem immediate mode set out to remove, now in application code, one frame late.

One engine, different wiring

The harness can show this directly, because some frameworks can be wired coarsely and finely on the same engine:

I benchmarked some of the engines in two ways, once in the most fine grained way they can be used, and once in a coarser way. The results show how much there is to gain with fine-grained reactivity.

Two things stand out. Iced’s factor is small because the view function still runs. And Floem’s coarse case is worth a look: every cell reads one global revision signal, which is notify in signal clothing. It is the slowest result on the chart. So signals do not rescue coarse state. The React team found the same thing from the other side: on a benchmark with “one giant input”, a signals-style runtime disappointed, and Joe Savona concluded the data model “is just as important, maybe more so” than the algorithm.30 The state has to be shaped like the reads. That is why I call this a state model problem. A good API should make it easy to align the data model with its UI projection.

Why run once

Suppose you accept all of that. You want the framework to track reads, and you want state shaped to match. What is the simplest API?

pub fn sidebar(threads: RwSignal<Vec<Thread>>) -> impl IntoView {
     Runs once, when the sidebar mounts.
    let unread = Memo::new(move |_| {
        threads.with(|ts| ts.iter().filter(|t| t.unread.get()).count())
    });

    Stack::vertical((
        Label::derived(move || format!("{} unread", unread.get())),
        dyn_stack(move || threads.get(), |t| t.id, thread_row),
    ))
}

That is the whole thing. The body runs once. The closures you hand to the framework run again when something they read changes. A local variable is a local variable. There are no hook rules, no dependency arrays, no stale closures and no PartialEq on props. Nothing reconstructs a row’s identity, because the row is still there.

Compare signals with re-running components, which is Freya’s model. It works well: one keystroke at 3,000 rows costs 1.2 ms. But look at a counter:31

#[derive(PartialEq)]
struct Counter;

impl Component for Counter {
    fn render(&self) -> impl IntoElement {
        let mut count = use_state(|| 0);
            }
}

use_state exists because that line runs again. You now hold both models: read tracking decides which scope re-runs, and then re-render semantics apply inside it, with hooks, prop equality and a diff. Finer updates need smaller components, which is GPUI’s problem at a much lower price. What the re-running body buys is ordinary control flow, and that is the serious objection.

Dan Abramov makes a compelling argument.32 Run-once puts your rendering logic in closures, so top-level control flow stops working, and you group code around values and not around logic. “The beauty of React is that making things ‘computed’ is an optimization, not a requirement.” He is right about it. This compiles, but the first line never updates:

Label::new(count.get()),               // read once; never updates
Label::derived(move || count.get()),   // a hole; updates

A reactive if has to become a dyn_container, and a for a dyn_stack. Solid 2.0 had to add dev warnings for top-level reads.33

But the same comment contains the reason I land the other way. He says Solid’s regrouping is “Similar to how you have to restructure your code around the values when you optimize it with useMemo.” Exactly. If your application never needs that, React’s model may be simpler. If it does, you pay for the regrouping either way, and the only choice is when: from the start, or later under a profiler. Ryan Carniato’s reply is the one I agree with: “In Solid you always write as if the data is derived so you don’t refactor to optimize.”32 Once you know you want this precision, run-once is the API that stops pretending otherwise. The failure modes also favour it. A forgotten hole goes stale on the first update, in the place you wrote it. A forgotten notify depends on what else happened to redraw.

To be perfectly honest, the ecosystem’s wider convergence is on read tracking in general, and not on run-once specifically. Angular considered per-binding updates and chose per-view, in writing, and it lands within about 1 ms of Solid on a partial update.6 34 Apple and Google, who control their languages, kept re-running bodies with @Observable and Compose.35 36 A hole is itself a re-run scope, so what differs is how big the default scope is. Two things I want to note on this though:

  • First, those systems pay for their larger scopes with a compiler. Compose has a compiler plugin, Angular compiles templates, and React’s compiler is the serious rival to everything here: it keeps React’s API and removes many needless re-renders, with loads up to 12% better.37 For Rust, I suspect that most people that prefer immediate mode or elm (or whatever GPUI is) would not like the idea of an additional compiler. A proc macro only sees tokens, not types, and render is an arbitrary function, so there is no pass that can split it into scopes. What Rust can express cheaply is a closure.
  • Second, their own guidance keeps describing the same problem: “Defer reads as long as possible” for Compose, and “Unnecessary view body updates can really add up” for SwiftUI.38 39 A framework that runs the body once removes that category at component level.

View-level rerun and fine-grained signals can have the same performance ceiling. But signals encourage fine-grained state projections and memoization from the beginning, for view-level rerun its an explicit choice that often leads to more boilerplate.

Signals do not automatically make your app fast

Fine-grained reactivity does not make an app fast on its own.

Floem’s reactivity does exactly what it promises. Changing a label runs 5 effects and spends 0.01 ms in reactive work, then about 14 ms in layout, because Taffy does not know that one leaf moved. (Floem also has a known bug where that edit never repaints, so treat this as a floor.) Vizia runs 4 bindings, then walks all 120,091 entities, for 46 ms. Slint writes an equal value in 4 µs, and takes 172 ms for a label, in a pass that walks about 30,000 items. Freya produces 5 mutations, then visits 57,050 layout nodes to recompute 14. GPUI beats most of them on this edit.

This is the distinction the argument depends on. All of those linear costs are in the engine respectively. Nothing in the application’s code requires them, so they can be fixed behind the same API without changing an application. zgui shows how far that goes: 0.69 ms for the label at 3,000 rows and about 0.26 ms per 1,000 rows, around 12 times flatter than GPUI. It is still not flat, and it is my framework and was tuned on this harness, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. In Iced and egui the linear cost is in the contract: the API says your code runs. No engine work can remove that, and app code has to change. GPUI probably sits somewhere in between, which is why gpui-fast can improve the situation to some extent.

At this point, I wan’t to share a more detailed benchmark matrix. Read the re-running columns down the first five rows and they barely move, because they do not depend on the edit. The signal columns move a lot, because the underlying implementations differ.

The bottom of that grid is also where the cost signals have becomes visible.

  • Creation. Filtering at 3,000 live rows takes 56 ms in Iced, 67 in egui and 123 in GPUI, against 371 in zgui, 835 in Floem and 982 in Freya. On a virtualized list it is 1.0 ms in Iced and 7.2 in zgui. “Setting up the dependency graph is not free.”6
  • Memory. Resident memory usage for large scenes is generally higher the more a framework retains.
  • Effects. Facebook moved away from two-way binding because “cascading updates” became hard to predict.40 That history is true, and Angular’s docs still say “Effects should be the last API you reach for.”41 Modern graphs are glitch-free. Careless effects are still difficult to reason about and quickly result in feedback loops or similar stuff.
  • Rust. Signals rely on arena handles and move closures. Levien thinks such patterns “adapt poorly to Rust”.3 I think they adapt well enough, and GPUI’s entities are arena handles too, but, admittedly, it is not a free lunch.

Conclusion

GPUI makes a full frame realitively cheap, and that makes it probably good enough for many use-cases. It is certainly enough for an editor whose expensive surface is handled by hand. For a large application it leaves a choice: keep the API people like and pay per view, or get precision by writing a signal graph out of entities. Elm and immediate mode have the same problem. Each is clearest in the small, and each loses the thing it was chosen for as precision becomes necessary, and, from my personal experience, that happens faster than people expect.

Tracked reads are where most of the field has ended up, whatever it started from. If that is where we are going, I think we should start there, and make the component a function that runs once.

Method

  • Numbers are medians of apply and settle from my unpublished harness, on one machine: i9-13900K, RTX 3080 Ti, Vulkan, Linux. Windows, compositor and input are not included. Frameworks’ maintainers have not reviewed the adapters.
  • GPUI is at ddc9eda925 and gpui-fast at 86a8228229. zgui is at 082337db. These were through September and November 2026, as the best of three passes.
  • Cells marked † in the grid failed their correctness oracle: Floem’s label and keystroke edits, as noted above, and Slint’s font size. Every other charted cell passed.
  • The 60-panel results are gpui-fast’s retained_bench with my additions, in test mode, so no GPU work is included. Retention off there is still gpui-fast.
  • Figures from Zed’s plan are its authors’, from experimental branches.
  • Rust examples were type-checked against the vendored frameworks. Vizia’s and Freya’s come from their own sources, shortened.

item.title: RIP, Harvest (429 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://aphyr.com/posts/427-rip-harvest, See on Hacker News

I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest.

Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines.1 I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.

Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons, the company that gutted Vimeo. I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.

Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.

I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.

Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?

item.description:
